prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength open a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B005 alone, with Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The round-1 exchange did not move me, it sharpened what I think the committee can say. All eight of us arrived at the same part and the same two names, but I do not treat that as evidence; what persuades me is that the mechanism can be written down in a few lines and checked. Choose the trapping wavelength so that the differential light shift of the clock transition vanishes, confine the atoms tightly enough that recoil and Doppler shifts disappear (Lamb-Dicke regime), and then interrogate thousands of atoms in parallel so that the quantum projection noise falls. That is a different mechanism from the comb, which counts optical cycles, and from the single-ion clock, which achieves accuracy by isolating one particle. In answer to the chair's first question, in one sentence: the lattice clock is the first scheme in which a many-particle ensemble is protected from the dominant perturbation by a design principle (the magic wavelength), so that accuracy and stability both reach the 1e-18 level together instead of being traded against each other. The remaining shifts (blackbody radiation, lattice hyperpolarisability, collisions) are quantitatively understood and have been cross-checked between laboratories, and the physical payoff is already visible in laboratory measurements of the gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings. The credit divides cleanly into the proposal and first realisation (Katori) and the record accuracy and many-body control (Ye).
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is still kind and novelty: a sceptic can call the lattice clock the best possible refinement of a lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and no violation of a symmetry or variation of a constant has been seen, only tighter bounds. I now think the many-atom point answers part of this, but not all of it: if a colleague insists that a Nobel discovery must be a new phenomenon, this part fails that test and I cannot argue otherwise. The second objection is credit. Two names cannot represent Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Derevianko and the ion-clock groups, and the committee should ask outside experts to verify Katori's 2001-2003 proposal against the first strontium lattice measurements before the vote. Third, the SI second has not yet been redefined; I do not regard this as a reason to wait, but it is a real reservation.

responses.point: Kroll weighs the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes and the credit beyond two names as real but not decisive, noting that the lattice-clock concept is distinct from both prior prizes, and that a redefinition of the SI second has not yet happened.
responses.response: I agree with your weighting and would add a reason for it. The comb and the ion clock each solve a different problem (counting optical cycles, and isolating a single particle), and neither contains the magic-wavelength idea, so the lineage is shared but the mechanism is not. On your point about waiting for the redefinition, I would ask what we learn by waiting. The redefinition is an administrative decision by metrologists that depends on comparisons already performed, and the physics we are judging is already complete: reproduced, compared over fibre links, and used for redshift and constants tests. Delay adds no new scientific evidence and only risks the committee appearing to follow the metrology bodies. Where I would push you is the primary-source caveat you raise yourself about accuracy figures from memory: that is a task for outside experts, and I would like it done before the vote.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the lattice clock is a clue from nature in his sense, since 1e-18 clocks already test constants, search for dark matter and resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres, but also worries that only tightened bounds and no measured variation or violation exist so far.
responses.response: I share the first half of your argument and the second half does not change my position. A null result that tightens a bound by orders of magnitude is a measurement about nature, and the redshift over a millimetre is not a null result: it is general relativity observed directly in a laboratory. Still, I accept your point that this prize would be recognised for an instrument and its performance, not for a finding, and I do not want to hide that in the citation. This is why I prefer a citation that names the invention and its mechanism, and does not promise discoveries that have not been made. If the committee requires a positive finding, then B005 is weaker than you or I would like, and I would then look at B014, but I do not think the mandate requires it.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, keeps B005 as the one-part configuration but lists B035 as the first alternative, asks whether a two-part prize combining B005 with one credited name from B035 would be acceptable, and notes that atomic physics lies outside their expertise so they rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson to confirm Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I would not support a two-part prize with a single name from B035. The IceCube credit is shared by Halzen, Karle and Spiering within a large collaboration, and splitting them is unfair to the omitted names, as you say yourself. I also do not see a scientific reason to add a second part: B005 is complete and uncontested in its two names, and a second part would be added for balance and not because it has been shown to be ready. On your reliance on the atomic-physics members, I come from the statistical-physics side and I read the pair as sensible, but I agree the chronology check belongs with experts and not with those of us who are adjacent to the field.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B005 first as atomic physics at its most elegant, with strong theory-experiment agreement, while flagging that the overlap with the comb and ion-control prizes may seem incremental to some colleagues.
responses.response: Your argument about theory and experiment is, for me, the strongest piece of evidence on maturity. I would use it in the citation discussion: the lattice-clock systematics are not only measured but computed (blackbody shift, hyperpolarisability, magic-wavelength values), and independent laboratories agree. Because you are closest to the atomic-physics community, I would ask you to say whether any of those calculations are controversial in a way that would contradict the 'understood' claim I am making.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a discovery in the Nobel sense, or as a precision-measurement invention, given that no violation or varying constant has been found.

Whether Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and first strontium lattice-clock measurements, checked against primary sources by outside experts, confirm the priority for Katori and Ye and the roles of Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Derevianko.
Whether delay for the SI second redefinition would add any scientific evidence; I think not, but colleagues who differ may have a point about the timing of the public signal.
I may be over-weighting mechanism and simplicity because of my own field, and I am not an atomic physicist; I have not checked the 1e-18 figures against the primary papers.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B005 or for Katori and Ye: my research is in statistical physics of complex systems and I have no collaboration with either. For my alternative B016 (KPZ) my work is in nearby non-equilibrium statistical physics, with no recorded collaboration with Kardar, Zhang or Spohn, and B016 is not in my preferred configuration. I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson (institutional proximity only). No change from round 1.
